items.title: Yankees get outplayed by Rasmussen, Rays in Game 1 of ALDS
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees came into the ALDS riding high, having crushed their archrivals in the Wild Card Series, the lineup coming alive just in time. Unfortunately, just as quickly as they woke up, the bats fell asleep, no match for Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in a 1-0 shutout loss to Tampa Bay.

New York’s downfall started (and in a way ended) when Gerrit Cole gave up a solo home run in the third, the primary blemish in what was a five-inning outing with five hits and one earned run. Cole left a changeup over the middle of the plate, and Jonathan Aranda sent a deep fly into the right-field seats:

Cole was replaced by Ryan Weathers, who made his return to the mound after a stint on the injured list with a left elbow injury, and didn’t allow the Rays’ offense to inflict any more damage. Paul Blackburn replaced Weathers in the bottom of the seventh and recorded one walk in 1.2 innings. Brent Headrick followed, who walked one batter before escaping with two runners on to end the eighth.

As for the Yankees offense, well, there isn’t much to speak of, as the lineup Boone sent out simply couldn’t make any headway against the Rays’ elite pitching staff. Rasmussen ended up pitching eight scoreless innings, allowing only one hit and two walks, completely shutting down the Yankees’ ambitions of getting ahead early in the series. Rasmussen kept the Yankees not just out of the run column, but blanked them in the hit column until the eighth, missing a no-hitter by just four outs as Austin Wells broke things up with a two-out double in the eighth.

Yet that moment also brought one of the most notable errors in the Yankees’ decision-making, with Wells attempting to stretch his double into a triple. His speed wasn’t enough to get him to third, and the Yankees’ catcher got thrown out to end the inning. Victor Mesa made the throw to shortstop Taylor Walls, who immediately tagged Wells as he went for the slide. An aerial view showed that third base coach Luis Rojas was trying to hold Wells up, so it really was just Wells inexplicably attempting to get to third base with two outs:

It’s worth noting that Giancarlo Stanton made his first appearance at the plate since April, pinch-hitting for Ryan McMahon, and sadly struck out in four pitches from Rays reliever Bryan Baker as the Yankees’ attempt at a ninth-inning rally went nowhere fast, Baker also striking out Ben Rice and getting Cody Bellinger to ground out to end the game.

Though the Yankees may be on the road and striving for a victory in Game 2, it remains to be seen whether Boone will change the lineup and experiment with other position players to shuffle the order. There wasn’t much to smile about today, with the small exceptions of Stanton’s cameo appearance, and the solid showing from Weathers after a layoff. Sunday will give the Yankees another day of rest to regroup. Hopefully, we’ll see a different result come Monday.

items.title: AL Division Series Game 1: Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees will kick off the Division Series from Tampa, with Gerrit Cole on the mound and Ben Rice leading off as the Bombers look to continue the chase for 28.

Going with yet another lefty-heavy lineup, the Yankees are going with Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second, Spencer Jones in right field, and Luis García Jr. at first over Paul Goldschmidt. The veteran first baseman may appear as a pinch-hitter, as may Giancarlo Stanton, who is on the roster again but won’t start.

Drew Rasmussen will get his second career postseason outing for the Rays, looking for a hot start to the series in Tampa Bay. The 31-year-old righty had a 2.67 ERA in 30 starts during the regular season. He’s posting a 2.86 ERA against the Yankees this season, allowing 14 hits and giving up seven earned runs in 22 innings.

We hope that you’ll come join us in the game thread as we kick off another postseason matchup as the Yankees race for the American League!

: Tropicana Field – St. Petersburg, FL

: 6:30 p.m. ET

: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY) | 95.7 FM / 620 AM, WESX 1230 AM (TB) ESPN Radio (national)

items.title: Yankees reveal lineup for Game 1 of ALDS vs. Rays
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The Yankees are set to continue their postseason run, and have revealed their lineup for Game 1 of the Division Series from Tampa Bay.

Ben Rice leads off for the Yankees after dominating the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, with expectations to continue his hot streak against the Rays. Bellinger will bat second with García Jr. in the hole, seemingly unchanged from the Game 2 lineup that secured the sweep against Boston.

Spencer Jones will hit cleanup in the order and start in right over Heliot Ramos, followed by George Lombard Jr. and Jazz Chisholm Jr., who will get the start at second over Anthony Volpe. Trent Grisham will notably get the start at center field, with Austin Wells unsurprisingly starting behind the plate.

As confirmed ahead of the postseason matchup, Gerrit Cole will start on the mound as the Yankees look to earn a series opener win.

Here’s a look at the Rays’ starting lineup, which puts Yandy Díaz in the leadoff spot followed by Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero.

items.title: A full breakdown of the Yankees’ Division Series roster
items.author: Dani Mohr
items.content:
The stage is set for the Postseason, and the Yankees have confirmed their 26-man roster for the American League Division Series.

There isn’t too much of a change from the Wild Card Series roster, but it’s worth noting that Aaron Judge is left out once again, and Ryan Weathers is available to step in as a reliever for the first time since late August. The lefty pitcher was placed on the IL with a left forearm flexor strain. The Yankees also left out third baseman Amed Rosario to make room for Weathers on the roster.

Here’s everything you need to know about each player and how they can propel the Yankees’ postseason run in the ALDS against Tampa Bay.

The Yankees will rely on Bellinger to give the offense some momentum, especially without Aaron Judge. He went 3-for-9 in the Wild Card Series with a home run that sealed the victory for the Yankees in Game 2. If he can stay hot in Tampa Bay, it should be enough to keep the Pinstripes on top.

A utilityman most likely to be deployed at third base, Caballero has the potential to be effective defensively and may get the start over Ryan McMahon. He finished September batting .163 with a .260 OBP, but didn’t get any at-bats during the Wild Card Series against Boston.

Jazz will likely play second in higher risk scenarios and alternate with Anthony Volpe. He went 2-for-3 with two runs and worked a walk in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.

After drilling a home run that helped the Yankees dominate Boston in Game 2, García Jr. will look to keep his numbers up against the Rays. He will likely alternate with Paul Goldschmidt, who does well against lefties.

Serving as a reliable option at first base, Goldschmidt brings a strong veteran presence that sets the tone for the younger guys on the roster. He worked two walks late in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series that gave Ben Rice the perfect setup for the grand slam.

After making his return from the IL in the Wild Card Series, Grisham will likely alternate at center field with Spencer Jones. It’s unclear if the Yankees will use him as a starter against Tampa Bay over Jones, but keeping him available to pinch hit could be the best option.

Following his postseason debut, Jones will likely continue to build off his momentum as the Yankees head to Tampa Bay. However, if he ends up struggling to make an impact offensively, it wouldn’t be surprising to see a pinch hitter like Stanton take his place in the order.

A standout in the Wild Card Series, Lombard Jr. instills confidence defensively while also remaining fearless at the plate. He went 4-for-8 against Boston with three runs, and can give the Yankees support towards the middle of the order.

Alternating with Caballero at third, McMahon is expected to make a start at least once against Tampa to test the options at third base.

Although he didn’t play a huge role in giving the Yankees insurance against Boston, Ramos will likely start at right field if the Rays throw out a left-handed starter and otherwise prepare to get hot off the bench in the ALDS. There’s also a chance that he alternates with Spencer Jones in the field. After a bit of a cold start in Pinstripes, Ramos finished September batting .255 with a .491 slugging percentage.

What else is there to say about Rice other than that he’s been the most clutch hitter for the Yankees without Aaron Judge? There’s no doubt we’ve seen the last of his electricity at the plate, and it’ll be very exciting to see how he matches up against the Rays.

Available as a backup for Austin Wells behind the plate, it’s unsurprising that Sánchez made the roster and has the chance to appear in a low-risk scenario.

Despite not getting the chance to hit in the Wild Card Series, Stanton will likely have a pinch hitting opportunity in the ALDS. One of the Yankees’ all-time leading playoff sluggers, with 18 homers, Big G might have his classic playoff moment that will leave the Rays stunned.

After hitting a sacrifice bunt in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series that helped set the Yankees up to shut down Boston, Volpe has the potential to shine against the Rays. He will alternate with Jazz at second, and we will likely see him get the start at least once in the series.

After jumpstarting the Yankees offense that totaled 18 runs in the two-game Wild Card Series sweep, Wells will look to bring the same energy against Tampa Bay. It will be fun to see him hopefully win an ABS challenge.

Maintaining his spot on the roster as the Yankees’ closer, Bednar wasn’t needed in the Wild Card Series but got some work to stay fresh in Game 2. He’ll be prepared to earn the save against Tampa Bay should the Yankees enter the ninth with a lead and continue the chase for 28.

After giving up a hit in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series and inducing a double play that ended the seventh, Blackburn is prepared to make an impact in quieting the Tampa Bay offense.

Getting the start for Game 1 of the ALDS, Cole will look to dominate the Rays in his first postseason outing since 2024. If needed, he will also likely be available for the Game 4 start.

Effectively shutting down Boston’s offense in the Wild Card Series, Fried will likely start Game 3 and hopefully keep the Rays’ offense at bay.

Maintaining consistency throughout the regular season, Headrick is expected to shine in a relief role throughout the postseason. He finished the regular season with a 2.18 ERA and 98 strikeouts over 78.3 innings. Headrick was used a lot, but did at least get three full days of rest going into today.

If we don’t end up seeing him in a starting role, Rodón is expected to come in as a reliever and shut down the Tampa Bay offense. He didn’t make an appearance against Boston, but if he can keep his numbers from September trending in the right direction, he’ll be lights out.

Dominating Boston in Game 1, and continuing his feud with seemingly the entire state of Massachusetts, Schlittler will surely be one of the Yankees’ most powerful weapons on the bump. The 25-year-old ace is poised to make his second career ALDS appearance as a starter for Game 2 and could be available for a decisive Game 5 should this series go the distance.

Taking a spot as a relief option if needed, Schreiber may take the mound in a low-risk scenario.

Giving up a run in 1.2 innings of Game 2 in the Wild Card Series, Warren will look to bounce back and silence the bats from Tampa Bay. One of the team’s core starters all year, Warren started transitioning into a role with the bullpen through a couple appearances in September and his presence as a multi-inning option is one of the reasons the Yankees can so confidently field an extended bench.

Positioned to make his first relief appearance since being reinstated from the IL, Weathers will be a crucial addition to this roster in place of third baseman Amed Rosario. He showed promising signs in his bullpen sessions, and we’ll expect him to be an essential factor in shutting down the Rays’ offense. Weathers was another starter alongside Warren making the shift over, though he has some experience relieving as he made 12 appearances out of the ‘pen in his rookie season with the Padres.

Securing his spot on the roster over Tim Hill, Yarbrough will be available as a low-risk option, and he could make an appearance on the bump if there’s a scenario where they need to get a reliever out of a jam.

items.title: Arizona Fall League 2026 preview
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The minor league season has officially concluded league-wide, with the Triple-A Championship Game on September 26th officially serving as the conclusion of the final game in Minor League Baseball in 2026. As thousands of players across all levels prepare for their offseason, there exists a handful in every organization who aren’t quite done with organized ball yet.

That is where we find the Arizona Fall League, which will be running for the 34th season since its founding in 1992 as an opportunity for an assortment of prospects to gain additional in-game experience. It’s often used by organizations to compensate for lost time due to injury, give experience to lower-minor prospects against stiffer competition, or to use it as an extra opportunity to tweak or introduce something in a low-stakes environment.

The Yankees have sent players of all shapes and sizes to this, from non-prospects deep into the organizational depth chart to highly touted prospects like Aaron Judge, Gleyber Torres, Jasson Domínguez, and Alfonso Soriano. Two years ago, current Boston rival Caleb Durbin got himself on the map with a huge performance, proving that this stage can positively impact prospect buzz.

For those unfamiliar with the format, the league’s 30 teams are divided into six AFL clubs, which have a 35-man roster and contain the contingents from five different organizations. It changes every year, so the one that the eight Yankees representatives will be going to is the , alongside prospects from the Twins, Rockies, Diamondbacks, and Nationals.

With the AFL officially kicking off today at 3:30 p.m. EDT in Glendale, let’s meet the eight-man Yankees contingent:

The prized prospect of the bunch, Dax Kilby will headline the group. The 2025 first-round pick stole headlines with an incredible 19-game cup of coffee in Single-A Tampa last August that vaulted him onto Top 100 lists and raised high expectations for his first full professional season at age 19, but such a season was doomed from the start.

A hamstring injury suffered early in spring held him out of the Spring Breakout game in March and delayed his season debut until May 28th, but there was still plenty of runway from there. Unfortunately, after taking just two at-bats, he suffered a setback that held him out an additional six weeks. He finally returned for good on July 17th, but was limited to just 36 total games in what was supposed to be a big season for him. It comes as no surprise, then, that he’s getting extra reps here in Arizona.

In his extremely limited time at Tampa this season, Kilby was effective, slashing .261/.448/.435 with a 143 wRC+ in 154 plate appearances. He boasts an extremely mature approach at the plate, walking in a quarter of his plate appearances, but has yet to really tap into the power. He’s above-average at pretty much everything, something you love to see from a 19-year-old, but you’re looking for the standout trait.

Something to monitor in this, aside from how he performs against older pitching, will be his defense. He’s never been considered likely to stick at shortstop, but is a good enough athlete to feasibly play second base, third base, or even center field. We’ll see if he’s moved around or if one of the best prospects in all of the AFL will just get to man shortstop the entire time.

Every year, you’ll see the Yankees send one or two guys to the AFL who don’t have much of a pro sample to go off of. This year’s version of that is Mack Estrada, the team’s 11th-round pick in 2024, who has just 4.1 professional innings through the first 2.5 seasons of his professional career.

Estrada is a guy that the Yanks invested a lot in, giving him a massive overslot of $640,340, the fifth-highest in the class, to get him out of a commit to go to Florida State out of junior college. He, like the rest of the team’s draft-year pitchers, was shut down to end the 2024 season, but went under the knife early in 2025 and missed the next season and a half due to Tommy John surgery.

He only got back to pitch in four games this summer with the FCL Yankees, where he struggled in a bunch of small, choppy outings. He’s spent the last two months in the complex, so we’ll see if he’s being utilized as a multi-inning guy in the AFL.

What can we expect from him? We don’t have data on how his stuff has looked post-TJS, but he’s more of a fastball/slider guy who was capable of getting it up to 96 on the heater in college. The Yankees love to tinker with young pitcher’s arsenals, so we’ll see if he has another offering or two.

A handful of the players in this year’s AFL contingent missed time in the last two years due to injury, but few were able to get back from those injuries with enough time to be as impactful as J.T. Etheridge was.

An undrafted free agent out of Louisiana in 2024, Etheridge started his pro career strong in the FCL in May 2025, but struggled after a promotion to Tampa late in the season. His 2026 started as more of the same, pitching to a 6.51 ERA deep into August. As a prospect without much invested in you, it’s a dangerous game to play going into an offseason with zero production above rookie ball at 25, which he’ll be in January.

The fact he’s here in Arizona, though, shows that he did make some progress. Something seemed to click in mid-August, when he suddenly became the unlikely ace of a Tampa team that came within a game of a Florida State League championship. In his last six starts, he allowed just one run in 27 innings with 38 strikeouts, including a pair of scoreless playoff outings. The decision to send him came before a few of these outings, so the belief might’ve been there even longer.

He boasted an impressive 32.9 strikeout rate with great whiff rates. He sits at 94 on his four-seam fastball and has both a sweeper and a slider that grade well above average. The damage off him primarily comes from the curveball and sinker, which he throws a combined 23 percent of the time. Expect him to tinker with those this fall.

While Kilby is the much more important prospect for Yankees fans to monitor this fall, I’d argue that the guy I’m most excited to see get extra reps here is Antonio Gomez. You may remember that name from a couple of years ago as a defense-first catcher whose bat never quite caught up with him. Yes, that is that same kid.

Gomez was floundering at Double-A Somerset in June 2025 when he was placed on the Development List. While that is usually a death sentence for any prospect, Gomez was different. Instead of being in organizational limbo, he was switching professions, going from a catcher with an 80-grade arm to a flamethrowing reliever. He made his pitching debut a month later and lit up the radar guns, but underwent elbow surgery after just four outings.

He returned this August and has just been trying to get into a rhythm as a pitcher. He’s only tossed 8.1 total innings across 10 career outings, so any experience he can get here in Arizona is extremely valuable. The thing that tickles your fancy about him is his alien fastball, which sits in the upper 90s with over 20 inches of induced vertical break, something you pretty much never see in the bigs:

A late addition to the roster, Anthony Mena signed as an older international signing in 2024 at the age of 19 and didn’t make his stateside debut until 2026 after two solid years in the DSL. In 2025, he struck out 57 in 45.2 innings with a 3.11 ERA.

The results were pretty rough in his 16.2 innings in the FCL early this summer, but he got an aggressive promotion to Tampa midway through the season after a mountain of injuries completely destroyed their pitching depth. His stuff hasn’t quite caught up yet, but he did pretty well after the promotion, allowing just three runs in 16.1 innings across five multi-inning outings.

He leans on his low-90s sinker, throwing it 44 percent of the time, while supplementing it with a changeup, slider, and curveball, with the latter two generating the best results.

Our last pitcher of the bunch, Chris Veach, is the only one who isn’t extremely early in their development as a Single-A pitcher. A 2024 undrafted free agent out of South Carolina, Veach graduated from Tampa in 2025 after a terrific season, pitching to a 2.53 ERA with 75 strikeouts in 57 innings.

This year has been a much more difficult season for him, but not because of anything on the field. The 25-year-old missed nine weeks with an undisclosed injury in the summer, shortly after earning a promotion to Double-A Somerset in June. He was only able to get into 25 games and throw 29 innings, but he excelled while doing so, pitching to a 1.86 ERA with 39 strikeouts to 10 walks. He’ll be 26 in a month and a half, so the extra development will be very helpful for him.

We don’t have arsenal stats for High-A and Double-A, but a look at Veach’s repertoire shows he utilizes a heavy diet of changeups that is backed up by a trio of fastballs. Things might’ve changed in the last year, but he threw a breaking ball just 0.8 percent of the time last season. Could that be something they ask him to work on in the desert?

Finally, to the position players. Core Jackson is the second-biggest name value prospect they’re sending to Arizona this fall. The 2025 fifth-round pick had a strong debut season in the system, splitting time between High-A Hudson Valley and Double-A Somerset.

Jackson, who turns 23 in eight days, slashed .262/.360/.459 with 41 stolen bases in 101 games across the two levels. He’s played an adequate shortstop, but has also gotten run at both second and third base. With Kilby on the roster, I can’t imagine he plays much shortstop this fall, even if both likely project as third basemen.

He was limited to just 101 games this year due to three very short stints on the injured list for minor ailments, which might be why he’s here. It could also be a big vote of confidence for an upper-minors infielder, who could be a good 2027 away from knocking on the door of the majors.

Our last Yankee heading to the desert is another 2025 draftee, and someone who managed to be one of the more unlikely 20/20 players you’ll ever see. Drafted in the 13th round out of West Virginia last year, it was a difficult debut season for West, who exclusively plays first base.

He slashed .226/.300/.394 with 20 home runs, 76 RBI, and 20 stolen bases in 124 games with Hudson Valley and suffered from a consistency issue. He’d have strong weeks, but immediately trade it with rough weeks. This is a guy who slugged .600 in the Big 12 just 18 months ago and was drafted for his slugging ability. The conditions in the AFL usually benefit offense, especially with the altitude. This guy could hit some moonshots if he gets a hold of one.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Dave Winfield
items.author: Kento Mizuno
items.content:
Before Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton, Dave Winfield (along with Dave Parker) was the definitive “Holy (bleep) that guy is huge!” star. Although his Yankees tenure was clouded by a tumultuous relationship with George Steinbrenner, Winfield deserves to be remembered as a great Yankee who made those 80s teams memorable despite never winning a ring.

: October 3, 1951 (St. Paul, MN): 1981-90

Winfield’s athletic abilities were already quite apparent in his youth. He starred in both baseball and basketball in high school and college. Following his time at the University of Minnesota, he was drafted by teams from not one, not two, but three pro leagues — in addition to MLB’s Padres and the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks, the NFL’s Minnesota Vikings took a flier on Winfield even though he hadn’t played college football. Thankfully, the hulking phenom chose the diamond.

The Padres thrust Winfield into the fire, having him skip the minor leagues entirely and placing him on their major league roster. While he wasn’t exactly a star from the word go, he was a productive regular almost immediately, hitting .277/.331/.383 (106 wRC+) across 154 PAs in 1973 as a 21 year-old. 

From there, Winfield continued to steadily improve, going from 1.9 WAR in ‘74, to 2.8 in ‘75, and 4.6 in ‘76. In 1977, he earned his first All-Star selection; he returned to the Midsummer Classic every year from then on until 1988. His pièces de résistance came in 1979, when he slashed .308/.395/.558 (161 wRC+) with 34 homers and a league-leading 118 RBI while winning a Gold Glove in right field. His 7.8 WAR paced the National League, even though he finished 3rd in MVP voting. Bet all the keyboard warriors were furi- oh right they didn’t exist back then. 

All this was more than enough to catch the eye of George Steinbrenner, who was eager to add another ring after consecutive titles in ‘77 and ‘78. In December 1980, the Yankees made Winfield the richest player in baseball with a ten-year, $23 million contract. Winfield almost made the Boss’ dream come true in ‘81, posting a 139 wRC+ in the strike-shortened regular season before showing out on both sides of the ball in the ALDS and ALCS. Here’s the large baseball man robbing Tony Armas of a home run in ALCS Game 2:

However, the season ended on a sour note for Winfield and the Yankees. The Dodgers won the World Series in six games, and Winfield was limited to just one hit in 22 at bats. In a show of poor comedic timing, he asked for the ball after his lone hit, a single. Needless to say, this did not sit well with George Steinbrenner, and the two would become bitter enemies for the remainder of Winfield’s time in the Bronx.

The 1981 season would be the Yankees’ only postseason appearance during Winfield’s tenure. However, that was no fault of Winfield’s, who kept producing at a high level well into his thirties. Although modern defensive metrics suggest that his sterling defensive reputation at the time wasn’t wholly deserved, there is absolutely no doubt about the quality of his bat.

In terms of batting average, Winfield’s best year came in 1984, when he locked horns with a young Don Mattingly for the AL batting title. The teammates were tied going into the very last game of the season, but Mattingly won the title by going 4-for-5, raising his average to .343, while Winfield went 1-for-4, finishing the year at a .340 clip. Here’s a clip of him from that year showing not only his sheer strength, but the impressive plate coverage that allowed him to hit for such a high average:

On the other hand, saber-enthusiasts like me would point to 1988 as Winfield’s best season in pinstripes. That year, he slashed .322/.398/.530 for a 157 wRC+, the fourth-highest mark in the majors. What makes this even more impressive is that he did this at 36 years old. To put this into context, Giancarlo Stanton was in his age-35 season when he surprised us all by posting a 157 wRC+ in 77 games last year. Now imagine him being just as good this year, except over a full season. Can you? I certainly can’t. Among all qualified seasons by batters aged 36 or above since 1947, Winfield’s 1988 ranks 19th, tied with 1971 Willie Mays and 2001 Edgar Martinez.

All told, in his time as a Yankee, Winfield hit .290/.356/.495 with 205 homers and 818 RBI. No matter how you slice it, he was worth every penny of his contract. And yet, George Steinbrenner, famously afflicted with a severe case of “what have you done for me lately”-brain, made it his personal mission to antagonize Winfield at every turn.

In 1985, after the Yankees faded late in the season and ceded the division lead to the Toronto Blue Jays, the cantankerous owner derided Winfield in the papers, saying, “Where is Reggie Jackson? We need a Mr. October or a Mr. September. Winfield is Mr. May.” In 1987, Steinbrenner began to withhold payments owed to Winfield to be donated to the Winfield Foundation, founded in 1977 to provide relief and opportunities to struggling families in his hometown of St. Paul. Steinbrenner accused Winfield of misappropriating funds for personal gain, circulating unfounded reports in the media in an attempt to undermine the star player’s credibility.

Ultimately, Steinbrenner would ruin himself in his quest to tarnish Winfield’s name. The Yankees owner made a deal with gambler and alleged Mafia associate Howie Spira, paying him $40,000 in exchange to dig up dirt on Winfield. Spira publicly accused Winfield of betting on baseball, and commissioner Fay Vincent launched an investigation. However, no evidence was found of Winfield ever betting on baseball; what uncovered was Steinbrenner’s clandestine deal with Spira. Vincent ordered Steinbrenner to resign as general partner of the Yankees and banned him from team operations for three years, and that was that.

At that point, Winfield had had more than enough. In May 1990, he waived his no-trade clause and accepted a trade to the California Angels, where he would play the following season as well. In 1992, at 40 years of age, Winfield played a crucial role on the championship-winning Blue Jays, hitting 26 homers and driving in 108 in the regular season, and coming up with the decisive blow in Game 6 of the World Series, an 11th-inning, two-run double. So much for the “Mr. May” moniker!

After three more years in the majors, two with his hometown Twins and one final year with Cleveland, Winfield called it quits. His career numbers are truly staggering; 465 homers, 3110 hits, and a .283/.353/.475 line over 23 seasons. In 2001, in his first year of eligibility, he was elected to the Hall of Fame.

Dave Winfield was a truly elite player who shone brightly in the Bronx. It’s a shame that he only had one chance to play in the postseason as a Yankee, but that shouldn’t cloud our appraisal of what he contributed to this franchise. For the better part of a decade, Winfield provided Yankee fans with top-level play, even as his teams could not quite reach October. He deserves to be remembered as one of the Yankees’ best free agent signings of all time, and just simply as a Yankees great.

items.title: Yankees must slay the three-headed monster atop the Rays lineup
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
This is where things get down to the brass tacks. The Yankees swept the Red Sox aside in the AL Wild Card Series, boat racing Boston by a combined score of 18-2, to fly into the ALDS with belief and positive momentum. It’s a whole other beast they’ll face in the Rays, their offense rolling into the postseason in far better shape than the Red Sox.

The Rays raced out to an AL-best 98 wins, significantly outperforming their Pythagorean win-loss thanks to one of the most well-rounded approaches in baseball. Despite sitting middle of the pack in runs per game (4.54) and slugging (.402), Tampa Bay’s offense still finished with the fifth-best wRC+ (104). Their offense has a clear identity built around power at the top, speed, and bat-to-ball prowess. They struck out the least (18.8-percent) of any team in MLB, which helps explain how they tied with the Brewers for the league lead in batting average (.258), and when paired with their AL-leading 164 stolen bases allows them to get the most out of the traffic they generate.

The ever consistent Yandy Díaz leads things off, coming off his fifth-straight season with at least a 120 wRC+. He played 154 games, slashing .293/.359/.446 with 22 home runs, 85 RBI, 93 runs scored, and a 125 wRC+ while continuing to be almost impossible to whiff and strike out. He has hurt the Yankees his whole career and that was especially true in 2026, when he batted .362 with a .944 OPS and 154 wRC+ in 51 plate appearances. The lone holes in his swing are against high-spin four-seamers from right handers up and in or middle-away, a pitch which Games 1 & 2 starters Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler specialize in.

Jonathan Aranda bats second coming off a season in which he batted .274/.358/.434 with 22 home runs, 92 RBI, 73 runs scored, and a 123 wRC+. However, the Yankees had his number all season, holding him to a paltry .427 OPS and 15 wRC+ in 47 plate appearances as they were able to strike him out 34-percent of the time. He has shown a willingness to chase the fastball above the zone, which happens to be a weapon pitch for all four of the starters the Yankees plan to roll out.

Those two set the table for the scariest threat in the Rays lineup: Junior Caminero. The third baseman became just the second player in MLB history after Eddie Matthews to post consecutive 40 home run seasons before turning 23. He added patience to his game in 2026, almost doubling his career walk rate to finish with a .276/.360/.524 triple slash line, 42 homers, 101 RBI, 100 runs scored, a 142 wRC+ and 5.3 fWAR while posting the highest average bat speed in the league. He holds his own against almost every pitch but does most of his damage against the heater and breaking ball. Just three of his home runs have come against the off-speed so I expect the likes of Max Fried and Carlos Rodón to feed him a steady diet of changeups down and away. Encouragingly, the Yankees were one of the few teams that managed to rein him in — in 54 plate appearances he managed just a .565 OPS and 51 wRC+ with Yankees pitchers getting him to pop it up on over 30-percent of his batted balls.

MLB stolen base leader Chandler Simpson figures to bat in the middle of the order. He was the only qualified hitter in 2026 to not hit a homer, but was also one of just seven qualified hitters to bat above .300, his 7.8-percent strikeout rate second-lowest in baseball. He’s joined in the middle of the order by Victor Mesa Jr., the rookie acquired from the Marlins over the winter and promoted mid-season to hit 14 home runs with a 128 wRC+ and 2.6 fWAR in just 79 games. Generally batting ninth is shortstop Taylor Walls, whose 74 wRC+ at first glance wouldn’t scare you yet he has managed to be a thorn in the Yankees’ side with a 120 wRC+ in 111 plate appearances over the last four years.

For the rest of the spots in the lineup, the Rays tend to go with a strict platoon. Liam Hicks usually bats cleanup against righties, the catcher posting a 130 wRC+ with as many walks as strikeouts since joining the Rays from the Marlins at the deadline, while Nick Fortes tends to start against southpaws. At second base, Richie Palacios owns a 113 wRC+ against righties while Ryan Vilade owns a 126 wRC+ against lefties. In center, Cedric Mullins is probably the one guaranteed soft landing spot against righties with his 80 wRC+, while Jonny DeLuca is a far more potent weapon when a lefty is on the mound (114 wRC+).

Put together, Kevin Cash can rely on guaranteed production at the top of the lineup while a deep bench gives him the opportunity to mix and match depending on the matchup. He has shown all season that he remains one of the best managers at putting his players in the best positions to succeed thus squeezing every drop out of the true talent level of the roster. You know the Rays are going to do all the little things right — taking the extra base, moving the runner over, getting the run in from home with less than two outs — which makes the three-headed monster atop the lineup their X-factor in this series.

items.title: AL Division Series Game 1 Preview: New York Yankees @ Tampa Bay Rays
items.author: Estevão Maximo
items.content:
Sweeping the Red Sox with two blowout wins was a joyous occasion, not to mention the tangible positive impact of setting up your rotation for the ALDS. The Yankees can begin the series against the Rays with Gerrit Cole as the Game 1 starter, which is only fitting considering Cole’s regular-season campaign in 2026 began and ended against the Rays, both times with a quality start.

Making his postseason debut this season, Cole will get the ball after nearly a week and a half off, his longest time between starts since returning from injury. In three appearances against the AL East champs in the regular season—the most he had against any single team—Cole averaged six innings and delivered a 2.50 ERA, enjoying success against a team not known for its home run pedigree.

Having last played a competitive meaningful game well before the end of the regular season, the Rays will set out to prove there is no rust in their game with Drew Rasmussen starting Game 1. Who better to represent what the Rays are all about than Rasmussen, acquired for the power-hitting Willy Adames as a swingman/backend starter, only to turn into one of the more dominant starters in the AL?

The postseason scenario and all that it entails could be seen as an opportunity to test the Rays’ resolve when it comes to their ace. Rasmussen was already dominant last season—part of what held him back from entering the conversation with the big boys was just how carefully managed he was by the Rays, who only let him reach or surpass 90 pitches twice in 2025. This year, Rasmussen has done that 17 times, including a career-high 114 pitches in a win over the Yankees just a couple of weeks ago—one in which perhaps the Rays gave a sign of their intentions with a trial run. With this extra leeway, Rasmussen managed to pitch 22 more innings than last season despite having one fewer start (31 to 30).

Rasmussen’s ability to go deeper into games than what we’re accustomed to seeing not only from him but also from the Rays as a team is of great value—especially if we are to read into regular season numbers. As much as the Yankees may have a better rotation, perhaps the biggest advantage in this series is in the bullpen. While New York had the second-lowest bullpen ERA in baseball, Tampa was only number 14. The key here, particularly looking at the postseason and a matchup with the Yankees lineup, is that the 95 home runs allowed by the Rays’ bullpen represented the third-highest mark in the bigs.

Then again, this is a Tampa team with the benefit of off-days between each of the first three games. One can only imagine how aggressive they might be willing to go with the likes of Bryan Baker, Cam Booser, and Kevin Kelly. While Baker is the closer, Booser gets the nod as the X-factor for the Rays in Game 1 and this series as a whole—the Yankees were 1-for-10 against him in the regular season, the one being an Austin Wells home run.

Booser’s importance stems from a complete lack of southpaw options for a team whose only other left-hander who finished the season on the active roster was Steven Matz. Garrett Cleavinger was cleared to be a part of the ALDS roster, but his 2026 numbers were quite bad, with an 89 ERA+ in 41.1 innings.

Unlike the Red Sox, all the Rays’ top starters are right-handers, allowing Aaron Boone to utilize his lefty-heavy lineup without fear, starting in Game 1 against Rasmussen. And if Booser can’t shut them down out of the bullpen, Tampa all of a sudden has an incredibly difficult mission to contain Ben Rice, Cody Bellinger, Luis García Jr., and company.

items.title: Drew Rasmussen headlines a deep Rays staff entering ALDS
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
After a thorough dismantling of the Red Sox in a Wild Card sweep, the Yankees are riding high. Their offense torched Boston’s pitchers, scoring 18 runs on 26 hits and swatting four homers in the two-game set. Next up is another division rival, the 98-win Tampa Bay Rays.

Tampa’s starting rotation finished second in the AL to the Yankees in ERA, though they did so in 56 fewer innings and with 176 fewer strikeouts. They’re expected to hand the ball to the perennially-underrated Drew Rasmussen in Game 1. The 31-year-old has posted a sub-3.00 ERA in each of his six seasons with Tampa, though a couple of those have been severely shortened by injury. He made 30 starts this year and tossed a career-high 172 innings, going 16-5 with a 2.67 ERA while leading the league in WHIP (0.913) and K:BB ratio (5.44). He finished the season particularly strong, allowing six runs over his last six starts. Of note, he threw a career-high 114 pitches in his last outing of the season, hinting that Kevin Cash, the notoriously short-leashed Rays skipper, may be looking for his ace to shoulder a larger burden than usual.

Like Cam Schlittler, Rasmussen’s top three pitches are all fastballs: a cutter, a four-seamer, and a sinker. All three have been lights-out; opponents hit .205 and slugged .326 against the cutter this season, the best they fared against any of the three. He mixes in a changeup that he threw 354 times without allowing an extra-base hit and, less frequently, a curveball and a sweeper. The only item missing from the two-time All-Star’s portfolio is postseason excellence — he’s made just one playoff start, back in 2021, in which he allowed three runs in two innings before getting the hook.

Cash has remained noncommittal on how he’ll deploy the rest of his pitching staff. Freddy Peralta, Nick Martinez, Griffin Jax, and Ian Seymour were Rasmussen’s rotation-mates and all are expected to feature in some capacity. After a nightmare first half with the Mets, Peralta rebounded nicely with the Rays. The right-hander went 5-0 with a microscopic 0.79 ERA over his last six starts of the year, earning AL Pitcher of the Month honors for September while regaining the form that saw him finish fifth in NL Cy Young voting last year and firmly entrenching himself in the playoff picture.

Martinez was one of the best value signings of the offseason, winning 15 games along with a 3.10 ERA on a one-year, $9 million deal. The 36-year-old faded a bit down the stretch, allowing 20 runs in 42 innings across his last eight starts, and it’s fair to wonder if his career-high 180 innings have caught up with him. The Rays converted Jax from a reliever to a starter midseason and the results were strong. He had a lower ERA in the rotation (3.14) than in the bullpen (8.00) but threw 75 pitches or more in just six of his 23 starts. None of those came in his five September appearances, meaning he’d likely be used more as a bulk arm than a true starter if he does get an October start. Seymour also began the year in the bullpen, though he topped 90 pitches six times after moving to the rotation. He’s the only southpaw of the bunch, a fact which could either make him an attracting starting option or a valuable multi-inning reliever against a Yankees lineup featuring a bevy of lefties. So, too, does the fact that he faced the Bombers in his final start of the season and shoved, holding them to one baserunner in five scoreless innings.

With the addition of a superfluous starter or two, the Rays’ bullpen will be a deep, veteran group. Bryan Baker is the team’s shutdown closer, posting a 1.44 ERA that trailed only Toronto’s Louis Varland among qualified relievers while tying for the MLB lead with 41 saves. His .203 BABIP is an outlier, though, suggesting some confluence of good luck and playing into a defense that graded out as the best in the AL by DRS. The last time Baker blew a save was back on May 13th. He relies primarily on a four-seamer against which opponents hit .125 with no home runs this season and a changeup that sits more than 10 mph lower.

Cash’s top setup option is Kevin Kelly, who appeared in a club-high 71 games. Kelly pitched to a 2.44 ERA on the season but struggled down the stretch, allowing seven runs in his last eight innings of work. Behind those two, the pecking order is less clear. Cam Booser has been the most effective lefty in the ‘pen, recording a sub-2.00 ERA in 41 innings. Fellow southpaws Garrett Cleavinger and Steven Matz had down years after strong 2025s, as did right-hander Cole Sulser. Casey Legumina is another righty option, as is Tyler Wells, who allowed three earned runs in 18 innings after coming over from Baltimore at the trade deadline.

Wells and Cleavinger ended the season on the IL with forearm tightness but each pitched an inning in a scrimmage Tuesday and could be in play. Tampa’s bullpen ERA of 3.99 is more middle-of-the-pack than the performance of its starters, but they still have clear lanes to get through the late innings.

In looking at the Rays’ pitching corps as a whole, Rasmussen looms large as their greatest differentiator. He’s a tough matchup for any team, but if the Yankees can get to him tonight with their third starter on the hill, they’ll do a great deal to puncture the Rays’ confidence and derail their winning formula. After Game 1, the Yankees will likely need to contend with a kitchen sink approach from Cash, who can be expected to make aggressive, matchup-based moves to put his pitchers in positions to succeed.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 10/3/26
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
Here we go again. After besting the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, the Yankees begin a Division Series matchup against the AL East champions for the second straight year in a row, this time drawing the Rays as opposed to last year’s Blue Jays. The tale of the tape is close between these two teams, the Rays narrowly winning the season series 7-6 after winning the second game of a doubleheader in their four-game series last week. The difference has been where the games have been played, as the Yankees were 2-5 in the Trop but 4-2 against them at Yankee Stadium. Overall the Rays have been the best home team in the league with a 55-26 record, but the Yankees are sending them a challenge as they get to start Gerrit Cole in Game 1 tonight despite having to run out two other aces in the Wild Card, and Cam Schlittler will start Game 2 having pitched to a sterling 1.16 ERA on the road this year. This could easily become a five-game heavyweight bout if the Yankees manage to steal one of these first two games before shifting back to the Bronx, and there’s some revenge on the line for Cole as well after the Rays spoiled his debut season in New York beating them in the 2020 ALDS.

We’ve got a lot to get through before gametime, starting with previews abound. Nick and Peter will both dive into the pitchers and hitters respectively that the Yankees have to worry about from Tampa Bay, and Estevao will preview Game 1 specifically as Cole lines up against Drew Rasmussen. The Arizona Fall League gets underway over the weekend as well, and Michael is on hand to go over the Yankees prospects participating. Kento looks back on the saga of Dave Winfield’s career as we celebrate his 75th birthday, and then we’ll be looking ahead to first pitch.

American League Division Series Game 1

New York Yankees at Tampa Bay Rays

TV: TBS/HBO Max, TruTV, Univision

Venue: Tropicana Field, St. Petersburg, FL

1. What are you expecting from Gerrit Cole tonight, and will we see Carlos Rodon used in relief of him?

2. Get your picks in for the other Division Series matchups: who wins between the White Sox/Guardians, Braves/Dodgers, and Padres/Brewers?
